name: Vector
definition: The genetic sign of the small form: many characters each reveal a partial situation, and together these ellipses form a broken, unpredictable but necessary line that maps one heterogeneous yet homogeneous world.
deamer_quote: "a very powerful image of the heterogeneity composing a homogeneous world" (p. 95)
deleuze_examples: Man of the West (Anthony Mann, 1958) — the neo-western 'skeleton-space' with missing intermediaries
The Wild Bunch (Sam Peckinpah, 1969) — the 'incongruous makeshift group' with a debt to discharge
NOTE: Deamer's Section II gives no film examples; these are Deleuze's own Cinema 1 examples (not cited by Deamer); attribution from memory of C1: 165-168, verify

scenes: Five interlocking episodes (Omar, Malek, Dando, Binj, Abu Elias) set in one Yafa district: the lead of one story walks through the background of another, so a single street holds several separate situations.
Malek, an undocumented worker, labours in a restaurant kitchen for his dying mother while the restaurateur's family plot runs on around him: two situations in one workplace.
Dando, a Jewish cop, searches the streets for his missing brother, crossing the Arab characters' lines without resolving them: ellipses carried from one episode into another.
The district itself (Muslims, Jews, Christians, Bedouin, three kinds of law) shown as a patchwork of locations rather than one encompassing milieu: 'Israels', not Israel.

operation: Cut between several characters on separate missions through one place, and let each thread leave a gap that another thread fills.
shot_criteria: One frame holds several independent people, vehicles or creatures in one shared space, each clearly moving along its own path or doing its own task, with no single centre.
queries: High overhead view of a busy intersection with cars and pedestrians crossing in many directions
Crowded restaurant kitchen with cooks and dishwashers each working at separate stations
Police officer questioning people on a neighborhood sidewalk, black and white
Apartment building facade at night with different people visible in separate lit windows
Crowded open-air street market, wide shot, vendors and shoppers doing different things
Aerial view of a railway junction with tracks branching off in several directions
Close-up of ants moving along several crossing trails on bare ground
Animated map with several dotted lines tracing separate routes across a country

name: Milieu
definition: The first sign of the large form: a fully determined geographical, historical and social situation (the Encompasser), laid out through establishing and extreme wide shots, whose characters' actions merely exemplify it.
deamer_quote: "The characters are one with the milieu and the milieu at one with the characters." (p. 99)
deleuze_examples: Nanook of the North (Robert Flaherty, 1922) — the ice field as encompassing milieu
The Grapes of Wrath (John Ford, 1940) — the Dust Bowl situation that determines the family's migration
NOTE: Deamer's Section II gives no film examples; these are Deleuze's own Cinema 1 examples (not cited by Deamer); verify against C1 ch. 9

section3.film: marxism today (prologue) (Phil Collins, 2010), with its untitled sequel
scenes: Archive footage of an East German classroom: a lecturer chalks a pyramid (director at apex, workers at the base) and writes 'exploitation' on the blackboard.
The lecturer turns 'exploitation' into 'exploitation?' after a student says his West German uncle owns a car and washing machine: a whole social system diagrammed in one frame.
Talking-head monologues of three former Marxist-Leninist lecturers recount life before and after reunification, the milieu traced along a time axis (S → S`).
The sequel: a present-day lecture on Capital in modern Germany, product versus commodity, echoing the archive classroom shot for shot.

operation: Open wide on the whole social and geographic world, and only then let people move inside it as expressions of that world.
shot_criteria: An establishing or extreme wide shot where the environment (town, landscape, factory, institution, classroom system) dominates and the people are small parts of it; or an explanatory diagram of a social order.
queries: Lecturer drawing a pyramid diagram on a classroom blackboard, students at desks, black and white
Extreme wide shot of an industrial town with rows of houses and factory smokestacks
Hunter in furs on a vast flat snow and ice field, wide shot, black and white
Workers streaming out through factory gates at shift change, high angle
Concrete wall and guard tower dividing a city street, wide shot
Rider on horseback dwarfed by desert mesas under a huge sky
Farming village in a valley seen from a hillside, wide establishing shot
Aerial view of housing blocks and roads stretching to the horizon

name: Binomial
definition: The second sign of the large form: the milieu splits into two opposed lines of force embodied by characters, and the film proceeds through duels (violent, romantic, political) converging on a final decisive one.
deamer_quote: "The film is pure action from beginning to end." (p. 100)
deleuze_examples: The Birth of a Nation (D. W. Griffith, 1915) — parallel then convergent montage towards the final duel/rescue
NOTE: Deamer's Section II gives no film examples; these are Deleuze's own Cinema 1 examples (not cited by Deamer); verify against C1 ch. 9

scenes: Sandra, in a yellow dressing gown, crosses the vast empty Ford shop floor to a photoshoot corner and drapes herself over a car.
Close-up: EQUAL PAY written in red lipstick across her belly, turning a cheesecake pose into a declaration of the strike.
Cut up to the glass-fronted office above the floor: the American boss flown in to break the strike turns and walks away, the duel won in a look.
Rita O'Grady leads the women sewing machinists against management, union, husbands and government: a whole film of duels on one gendered line of force.

operation: Split the world into two sides, give each a face, and cut back and forth between them until they meet in a confrontation.
shot_criteria: Two opposed parties (people, groups, animals) visibly face or confront each other in the frame, or one side stares down the other across a clear divide.
queries: Woman in a swimsuit posing on a car on an empty factory floor
Manager looking down through a glass-walled office window over a factory floor
Striking women workers holding placards outside factory gates, black and white
Rows of women operating sewing machines in a factory workroom
Two boxers facing off in the ring, medium shot
Two rams butting heads on a rocky hillside
Tug of war between two teams on a grass field
Cartoon cat and dog squaring off nose to nose before a fight

name: Imprint
definition: The genetic sign of the large form: a complex milieu is internalised by a character, accumulating as pressure until it explodes into action, and made visible through an emotional object that links the character to the situation.
deamer_quote: "an indelible impression of the world upon a character" (p. 101)
deleuze_examples: On the Waterfront (Elia Kazan, 1954) — Kazan's behaviourism of internal factors
East of Eden (Elia Kazan, 1955)
Godzilla (Ishiro Honda, 1954) — subject of Deamer's own essay 'An imprint of Godzilla' (cited in front matter)
NOTE: Deamer's Section II gives no film examples; these are Deleuze's own Cinema 1 examples (not cited by Deamer) (Kazan per C1: 157-159, verify)

scenes: Mia dances alone in an abandoned flat with ripped wallpaper and tatty carpet, trying to exhaust the rage the estate has loaded into her.
Near some caravans Mia finds a thin, chained-up horse and keeps trying to free it; its death later releases her tears: the emotional object.
Left behind by Connor, the 'California Dreaming' CD spins on at the audition as Mia walks off the stage.
On the estate Mia interrupts girls dancing for the lads and their dogs and it ends in a head-butt: one of the local duels that fill her up.

operation: Load the character with the world scene by scene, give that pressure one object to hold, and let the release come late and violently.
shot_criteria: A lone figure visibly weighed down by their surroundings, or a charged personal object (toy, record, photo, animal) shown in close relation to a person, so the environment reads as pressing on them.
queries: Teenage girl dancing alone in an empty room with peeling wallpaper
Thin horse tethered on a chain in a field beside caravans
Close-up of a record spinning on a turntable
Girl standing alone at the foot of tall public housing tower blocks
Woman holding a child's shoe against her chest, close-up
Man sitting on a bed staring at a photograph in his hands
Giant reptile monster towering over a burning miniature city
Dock worker with a grim sweating face in close-up, black and white

name: Plastic figure
definition: Deamer's first sign of composition of the attraction-image: a small-form film is transformed by the large form, so an on-screen action, object or episode works as metaphor, metonymy or synecdoche for an implied situation that stays in ellipsis.
deamer_quote: "an object which has a meaning beyond itself" (p. 107)
deleuze_examples: Strike (Sergei Eisenstein, 1925) — the massacre of workers intercut with a slaughtered bull

NOTE: Deamer's Section II gives no film examples; these are Deleuze's own Cinema 1 examples (not cited by Deamer); attribution from memory of C1 ch. 11, verify. Also note Deamer's table Fig. I.18 lists Theatrical first and Plastic second, the reverse of his Section II text

scenes: In drought-stricken Kaohsiung, Shiang-chyi sees hundreds of watermelons floating in the sluggish Love River: the fruit replaces water.
Alone, she pushes a watermelon under her top and mimes pregnancy and birth.
Shiang-chyi finds her lost suitcase key set into the tarmac, but even when retrieved it will not open the case.
Garish musical numbers break in: a merman in a water tank, dancers with umbrellas in a dragon waterpark, costumes in watermelon green, red and black.

operation: Let one object or eruption stand in for the situation you refuse to show directly.
shot_criteria: A single object, creature or staged spectacle clearly standing in for something larger (metaphor/metonymy), for example fruit in place of water, animal slaughter in place of massacre, or a sudden stylised musical number.
queries: Many watermelons floating in a slow muddy river
Woman eating a slice of watermelon, close-up
Chorus line of dancers with umbrellas in a colorful musical number
Cattle being slaughtered in a stockyard, black and white
Dry cracked mud of an empty reservoir bed during a drought
Close-up of sand running through an hourglass
Chess pieces knocked over on a chessboard, close-up
Time-lapse of a flower wilting and drooping in a vase

name: Theatrical figure
definition: Deamer's second sign of composition of the attraction-image: a large-form film is transformed by the small form, so the real situation is expressed through a sustained fictitious action (allegory, myth, parody) that prefigures and keeps deferring the real action.
deamer_quote: "a sequence of images as precursor of the real action" (p. 107)
deleuze_examples: To Be or Not to Be (Ernst Lubitsch, 1942) — theatrical performance prefiguring real action
NOTE: Deamer's Section II gives no film examples; these are Deleuze's own Cinema 1 examples (not cited by Deamer); attribution uncertain, verify against C1: 182-183

section3.film: Scott Pilgrim vs. the World (Edgar Wright, 2010)
scenes: In a vast warehouse club Scott, flaming samurai sword in hand, cuts through Gideon's henchmen, who burst into showers of coins as points float up.
Horizontal split-screen of the two rivals' faces, then a slow-motion mid-air sword clash haloed in white light, with sound rendered as graphics.
Each evil ex is fought as a video-game level; beaten bodies dissolve into coins and Scott earns extra lives.
Comic-book effects: a punch launches a man into the sky, a giant mallet appears from nowhere, a sword emerges from Scott's chest.

operation: Stage the real conflict as a game, play or mock battle, and repeat it until it stands in for the fight itself.
shot_criteria: A visibly staged, rehearsed, cartoon or mock version of a conflict (drill, puppet fight, stage duel, war game, animated battle) standing in for a real one.
queries: Cartoon hero sword-fighting a villain at the top of a tall staircase
Rock band playing on stage in a crowded warehouse
Puppet show with two puppets fighting in front of an audience of children
Officers moving toy soldiers across a sand-table battle model
Children in costumes acting out a sword fight on a small school stage
Civil defense drill with volunteers pretending to be injured on stretchers
Soldiers storming a mock village during a training exercise
Two fencers lunging at each other in a gymnasium, black and white

name: Mise en abyme
definition: Deamer's own name for the genetic sign Deleuze leaves unnamed: plastic and theatrical figures nest inside each other so we cannot tell which form contains which, an image within an image within an image.
deamer_quote: "It is as if we enter and become lost in a hall of mirrors" (p. 108)
deleuze_examples: None: Deleuze neither names nor describes this sign (Deamer, p. 108)

scenes: Time freezes on the commuter train: the camera tracks back down the carriage past passengers stuck mid-laugh, a comedian mid-punchline and spilt coffee hanging in the air.
Colter Stevens wakes, again and again, in a replica helicopter cockpit, a plastic figure of the place he died that holds together and decays with his consciousness.
The same eight minutes on the train, re-entered repeatedly with variations: a theatrical figure that becomes a new real.
His real body, a bagged and tagged mutilated trunk on life support, is revealed as the ground beneath both figures.

operation: Nest the scene inside a replica of itself (screen, model, mirror, loop) until the frame and the framed trade places.
shot_criteria: An image visibly contains another image or replica of itself or its world: a screen showing a screen, mirrors facing each other, a model within the scene, a film being shown inside the film.
queries: Television set displaying an image of a television set
Two facing mirrors making an endless corridor of reflections
Camera tracking down the aisle of a train carriage past seated passengers
Pilot in a helicopter cockpit, close interior shot
Projector beam in a dark theater, audience watching a film on screen
Cameraman filming another cameraman who is filming him
Model railway with a miniature train passing through a tiny town
Artist at an easel painting the room he is sitting in

name: Figure of the sublime
definition: The first sign of composition of the inversion-image (SAS becomes sAs): a visionary character dreams up an action far larger than the situation requires, so the over-reaction exposes the situation, and the plan, as futile.
deamer_quote: "a film in which the behaviours of the character overwhelm the givens of the situation" (p. 111)
deleuze_examples: Aguirre, the Wrath of God (Werner Herzog, 1972) — the conquistador's mad river expedition
Fitzcarraldo (Werner Herzog, 1982) — hauling a steamship over a mountain
NOTE: Deamer's Section II gives no film examples; these are Deleuze's own Cinema 1 examples (not cited by Deamer) (C1: 184-185)

scenes: Grainy 4:3 video, front-on at eye level: Waj sits cross-legged before a faded wall-hanging holding a Kalashnikov (actually a toy; he says he has 'big hands') for his martyrdom video.
A cell member dies in an accident with homemade explosives, a dry-stone wall and a flock of sheep.
Waj and Hassan shake their heads continuously to blur the CCTV cameras.
At the training camp Omar fires the rocket launcher backwards and blows up the camp during a drone strike.

operation: Give a small person an absurdly grand plan and film the plan's execution with total solemnity.
shot_criteria: A visible act of grandiose over-reach or zealous spectacle, oversized relative to its means or setting: a lone zealot, a doomed grand machine, a mass rally, a stunt that fails.
queries: Man sitting cross-legged on the floor holding a rifle, speaking into the camera
Explosion in a field scattering a flock of sheep
Soldiers firing a shoulder rocket launcher with a big backblast of smoke
Massed troops goose-stepping past a huge rally stand, black and white
Men hauling a large boat up a steep jungle hillside with ropes
Inventor's homemade flying machine collapsing on takeoff
Lone preacher shouting on a soapbox to an indifferent street crowd
Daredevil going over a waterfall in a barrel

name: Figure of enfeeblement
definition: The second sign of composition of the inversion-image (ASA becomes aSa): weak, aimless characters whose futile acts, shrunk to specks against the horizon, reveal an immense and indifferent world.
deamer_quote: "weak characters reveal the sublime nature of the world" (p. 112)
deleuze_examples: Stroszek (Werner Herzog, 1977)
The Enigma of Kaspar Hauser (Werner Herzog, 1974) — the 'weaklings and idiots'
NOTE: Deamer's Section II gives no film examples; these are Deleuze's own Cinema 1 examples (not cited by Deamer) (C1: 185-186)

scenes: Three young men sit in silence at a round glass café table on a sunny square, a fountain jetting behind them; one checks his phone, one twirls a dead leaf, one yawns and stretches.
Characters wander Islamabad's streets alone or stare vacantly over the cityscape from the hills and tall buildings.
A ceiling fan overdubbed with helicopter sound: borrowed cinema standing in for experience.
On the way to the airport Hasan's car pulls level with an open-backed truck carrying an itinerant worker, and the class structure suddenly becomes visible to him.

operation: Shrink the character in the frame and give them nothing to do, until the world around them becomes the event.
shot_criteria: A small, idle or powerless figure visibly dwarfed by a large setting, or people shown doing nothing (sitting, waiting, drifting) while the environment dominates.
queries: Three young men sitting idle at a cafe table beside a fountain
Man standing on a hilltop looking out over a sprawling city
Laborers riding in the open back of a truck along a highway
Tiny figure walking toward the horizon across an empty plain, extreme wide shot
Lone man wandering an empty city street at dusk
Small rowboat dwarfed by huge ocean waves
Tramp sitting on a park bench feeding pigeons
Close-up of a beetle stuck on its back struggling on the ground

name: Quotidian
definition: Deamer's name for the unnamed genetic sign of inversion, where sublime and futile become 'the same thing': everyday situations and actions at once trivial and immense, the universe indifferent yet the only ground of action.
deamer_quote: "the pettiness of our function is the heroism of life" (p. 113)
deleuze_examples: No film named: Deleuze only notes sublime and enfeebled can become 'the same thing' (C1: 186, via Deamer p. 110)

scenes: Sunlight spreads across bright white net curtains while Adam sits across a wooden desk from the new manager, who takes notes during his job interview.
A long night take of Adam on his motorbike, the headlight sweeping the white walls of an alleyway.
Adam at his window, sun on his bare torso, lets the curtain fall back to shut out his son being taken away for the army.
Adam and his wife feed each other watermelon while war footage plays on the TV; at the end dead leaves float on the abandoned hotel pool.

operation: Hold a static medium shot on an ordinary gesture long enough for the world outside the frame to press in.
shot_criteria: An ordinary, unremarkable daily activity or domestic/work space filmed plainly and patiently (curtains, desk, pool, meal, commute) with nothing dramatic happening in frame.
queries: Sunlight shining through white net curtains over a large window
Man being interviewed across an office desk by a manager taking notes
Motorcycle headlight moving through a narrow whitewashed alley at night
Dead leaves floating on the surface of an empty hotel swimming pool
Couple eating dinner at home while watching television
Attendant skimming a swimming pool with a long net
Woman hanging laundry on a clothesline in a backyard
Commuters waiting at a bus stop in the early morning

name: Limit of the large form action-image
definition: The first sign of composition of the discourse-image: the given milieu hides a question, and the character has to draw out that problem before any action can be a considered response rather than an explosive reaction.
deleuze_examples: Seven Samurai (Akira Kurosawa, 1954) — what is a samurai today?
Ikiru (Akira Kurosawa, 1952)
Dersu Uzala (Akira Kurosawa, 1975)
NOTE: Deamer's Section II gives no film examples; these are Deleuze's own Cinema 1 examples (not cited by Deamer) (C1: 188-190)

scenes: US and Mexican planes fly over the Infected Zone laying poison into the jungle below.
In the zone people smugglers have Scoot and Whitney sniff the air: the gas masks protect against the American chemicals, not the aliens.
A huge metal fence cuts across the continent and a concrete wall seals the US border; inside, towns are overgrown by jungle, and the pair come across an ancient Mayan temple.
At a deserted Texas gas station two luminous aliens twine their tentacles in the night sky, the creature's 'attack' revealed as a search for its mate, and the humans kiss.

operation: Set up the fight, then turn the camera until the audience is no longer sure which side is the monster.
shot_criteria: A situation built for conflict (wall, poison, masks, hunting, evacuation) whose image makes the aggressor/victim relation ambiguous or reversible; the frame raises a question instead of showing a duel.
queries: Crop duster plane spraying chemicals over a forest canopy
People wearing gas masks walking through dense jungle
Tall barrier wall stretching across a desert landscape
Ancient stone pyramid temple overgrown by jungle
Abandoned village houses overgrown with vines and vegetation
Two octopuses entwining their tentacles underwater
Refugees carrying bundles walking along a road out of town
Hunter and wild animal facing each other in a forest clearing
